analysis.title: UBS Global I/O Semiconductors: New US Export Controls on Cloud Access; Assessing the Impact
key_insights: The US Commerce Dept Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) posted a new rule on remote (cloud) access to advanced semiconductors. UBS's experts, including a former Commerce official, say it tries to do what the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule attempted but never took effect.

The rule was written by, and at the direction of, the Treasury Department, which UBS's experts call atypical. UBS cannot say it responds to the NVDA situation, but calls the timing highly coincidental and flagged the risk in its estimate cuts the previous morning.

Current export controls require no license for shipments to Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Singapore. Data center construction in Malaysia has grown sharply as a result. Press reports cite about 2GW online in one province, about 10GW under construction and about 25GW approved in total, backed by US and Chinese hyperscalers.

UBS assumes shipments into Malaysia alone run at a few GW per year, with about half going to China-domiciled companies per the NYT. The rule carves out online retailers and social media companies, but UBS expects US companies to act conservatively unless they are continuously assured of the end customer.

UBS estimates the rule could remove 1-2GW of current demand, mostly NVDA. At $30B+/GW this is roughly consistent with UBS's estimate of a 10% demand impact. NVDA could redirect shipments to other customers, so UBS sees it as more of a longer-term issue, especially if powered shell permitting in the US tightens.

Experts see higher odds that the MATCH Act passes, possibly attached to the NDAA in the coming Congress. Timing remains the key question, and the US may not want further export controls right after the cloud access rule.

One expert believes the gap between what ASML, TEL and other foreign suppliers sell into China and what US equipment suppliers sell is small, so MATCH would mainly create tension with the Netherlands and Japan.

MATCH would use the Foreign Direct Product Rule (FDPR) to level the field. Open questions are who decides which Dutch and Japanese tools are equivalent to restricted US tools, and what incentive those governments have to comply. An expert said FDPR use could upset allies more than tariffs.
A contemplated ban on immersion DUV would make supporting trailing-edge fabs and lines in China difficult, with possible spillover across the industry, including outside China.

ASML and Japanese suppliers would be most directly hit by MATCH. In UBS's coverage only KLAC is seen as indirectly and negatively affected, because of its high attach to litho process steps. Others are affected less, though less litho could mean fewer deposition and etch tools.

NVDA is the most directly affected by the cloud rule, and the whole supply chain from memory to semiconductor equipment would be hurt by closing a large demand corridor. Over the longer term, MATCH could benefit memory suppliers outside China by constraining Chinese capacity additions.

market_movers.rationale: Most directly affected by the cloud access rule. UBS sees 1-2GW of demand at risk, consistent with its 10% demand impact estimate. Diversion to other customers should limit near-term damage.
The only covered name UBS sees as indirectly hurt if MATCH passes, because of its high attach to litho process steps.
ASML and Japanese suppliers would be most directly impacted if MATCH passes and FDPR is applied to foreign tool sales to China.
Over the longer term MATCH could benefit memory suppliers outside China by constraining Chinese capacity additions. The cloud rule itself hurts memory demand.

sector_views.rationale: The cloud access rule could cut 1-2GW of AI chip demand, and MATCH Act odds have risen. UBS sees negative read-across from memory through equipment, with memory outside China a possible long-term beneficiary of MATCH.

risk_factors: Loss of 1-2GW of near-term AI chip demand, mostly NVDA

Timing of any MATCH passage is uncertain
